title: Al-Khwarizmi and the Invention of Algebra
summary: Tells the story of al-Khwarizmi, a mathematician who worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad during the Islamic Golden Age and wrote an influential book that gave the world algebra, new number signs, and, through his own Latinized name, the word algorithm.
poll: Al-Khwarizmi's work on algebra was one of the most important mathematical achievements in human history.

versions.title: Al-Khwarizmi and the Invention of Algebra
versions.text:
A man lived long ago. His name was al-Khwarizmi. He lived in a city. He was good at math. He liked hard problems. He liked to think.

He wrote a book. The book was about math. It showed how to solve problems. We call this math algebra now. It is still used today.

The word algebra comes from his book. His book used plain words. It did not use plus signs. It did not use equal signs. It just used words.

He also helped bring new signs for numbers. The signs made math easier. We still use signs like these. They are a big help.

Traders used his math to sell things. Builders used it to measure land. It helped many kinds of work. It helped many people too.

Later, other people read his book. They learned his math too. His name even gave us a new word. That word is still used now.

versions.title: Al-Khwarizmi and the Invention of Algebra
versions.text:
A man named al-Khwarizmi lived long ago in Baghdad, a city that served as one of the great centers of learning and scholarship during that remarkable era. He worked as a mathematician inside a renowned institution known as the House of Wisdom, where scholars from many lands gathered to study and share ideas. He was especially fascinated by solving number problems that other thinkers had struggled to work out.

He wrote a mathematics book that carefully explained, step by step, systematic methods for solving a wide variety of tricky equations. We still call this entire branch of mathematics algebra today, a name taken directly from a word in his original book. Scholars across the known world continued studying his groundbreaking ideas for many centuries afterward.

The word algebra actually comes from an Arabic word, al-jabr, used in the title of his influential book. Rather than relying on modern number signs or symbols, his book explained every mathematical idea using plain, carefully chosen words. It did not use plus signs, minus signs, or equal signs of any kind.

Al-Khwarizmi also helped introduce a practical new system of number signs, including the powerful concept of zero, into his home region. These signs made adding, subtracting, and solving complicated problems dramatically faster than the older, clumsier methods people had relied on before.

Traders throughout the region used his careful methods to calculate prices and divide goods in fair, honest ways. Builders and surveyors used his mathematics to measure land accurately before constructing new homes and public buildings. His practical ideas quietly transformed many different kinds of everyday work across a vast stretch of territory.

Centuries later, European scholars eagerly translated his influential book into Latin and other languages. This slow, patient work of translation helped his mathematical methods spread across an entirely different continent. His own name, Latinized over time, even gave the modern world the word algorithm, a term still essential to computer science today.
